title: Nobel laureate Francis Halzen says a galactic supernova would hand IceCube a million neutrino events — and Wisconsin another Nobel
excerpt: Francis Halzen, the University of Wisconsin physicist who shared the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for building IceCube, says the cubic-kilometer…
content:
The first thing Francis Halzen wants you to understand is that he did not build a telescope. He built an eye — one that sits 1.5 kilometers down in a moving glacier at the South Pole, weighs nothing you could weigh, and sees particles that pass through the entire planet without noticing.

The second thing is that the machine almost did not get built, three separate times, and one of those near-misses turned out to be the thing that will likely define the next two decades of the field.

Halzen, a University of Wisconsin particle theorist, shared the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for originating the idea of Antarctic ice as a detection medium, proving it with a prototype called AMANDA, and leading the detector, IceCube, that produced the first evidence of cosmic rays from outside our galaxy. He laid out how it works on Cleo Abram's HUGE Conversations — and kept returning to the gap between what the machine was designed to do and what it actually delivered.

Why the neutrino is the only messenger that arrives undeformed

Light is blocked by matter. Cosmic rays carry an electric charge, so magnetic fields bend their paths as they travel — which is why, for a century, nobody could pinpoint where they came from. Gravitational waves tell you something violent happened, but not what.

Neutrinos have essentially no mass and no charge. They pass through stars, planets, and the detector itself without being absorbed or deflected, which means they arrive pointing back at their origin.

"The fact that they interact means that they can escape from places in the universe where light doesn't get out," Halzen says. His example is the sun: a photon born in the core ricochets for tens of thousands of years before it escapes, while a neutrino leaves instantly and reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

The price of that passivity is near-invisibility. Roughly one in a million neutrinos streaming through IceCube actually strikes anything. Everything about the machine follows from that number.

5,160 sensors, 86 holes, one cubic kilometer of ice

IceCube is an eye that looks at the sky but sees neutrinos. The surface station at the South Pole is only a computing center; the instrument hangs in the ice below, floating along inside a glacier that shifts about 10 meters a year.

ComponentSpecification
Sensor strings (boreholes)86
Sensors per string60
Total light sensors deployed5,160 (about 1 in 100 lost during deployment)
Instrumented volume1 cubic kilometer
Sensor spacing25 meters apart
Depth1.5 km below the geographic South Pole (under 3 km of total ice)
Sensor typePhotomultiplier tube in a glass pressure vessel

The mechanism is surprisingly simple to picture. A neutrino occasionally hits a nucleus in the ice, turns into charged particles, and those particles emit a cone of blue light. The sensors record the glow; the shape and timing of that cone let physicists reconstruct both the energy of the original neutrino and the direction it came from. Stack up enough events and you get a map of the sky.

Three ways the project nearly died — and the ice turned out to be better than anything made in a lab

Halzen tells the story as a chain of obstacles that each could have ended it.

The first was whether Antarctic ice is optically clear enough to see the glow at all. AMANDA, a prototype with 1–10% of IceCube's capability, answered that. Blue light travels 100 meters or more through the ice, versus about 8 meters in the purer kinds of ice that can be manufactured in the lab. "You can actually not find a solid that clear even if you try to build it in the lab," he says. The ice is snow that fell 50,000 years ago and compacted into an ultrapure solid. That clarity is the single reason sensors can sit 25 meters apart instead of touching.

The second was the drilling. Glaciologists had hot-water drills that could carve a coffee-cup-wide hole a few hundred meters deep; IceCube needed a basketball-sized borehole two and a half kilometers down. Engineers told the team repeatedly that a hose that long would collapse in its own boiling water. One engineer eventually found a company near Padua, Italy, willing to build it. "For weeks I thought this project is finished," Halzen says.

The third problem is the one with the biggest payoff, and it was a failure. Atmospheric neutrinos produce a permanent background Halzen compares to clouds in the sky. The original plan was to deploy at 1 kilometer down; that depth failed because of bubbles in the ice. Going deeper fixed it.

But the abandoned shallow detector could do something IceCube cannot: it can register supernovae anywhere in the Milky Way, because a supernova produces a uniform wash of neutrinos rather than a single energetic event.

My colleagues refer to this as if they serve you lemons, you make lemonade," Halzen says. "So we discovered that we could actually use detector at 1 kilometer to detect supernova."

That accident now stands at the center of the field's near future. IceCube has run continuously since 1994, so the team can guarantee there has been no galactic supernova in that entire span. If one occurs, the detector would log about a million events and assemble a detailed movie of what happens inside the collapsing star — an observation Halzen says half-jokingly could earn Wisconsin another Nobel Prize.

The discovery paper was published with a deliberate refusal to overclaim

After AMANDA, the team went hunting for "guaranteed neutrinos" from a theorized source and found nothing. But the same data contained two spectacular high-energy events that could not have been generated in the atmosphere.

A normal experiment would have issued the headline. This one did not. There is no second detector anywhere to cross-check the result, and Halzen's team understood that credibility is a nonrenewable resource.

"There is no second detector to check us," he says. "We realized if we ever made a claim that turned out not to be true, then nobody would actually ever believe anything we did after."

So the collaboration published the two events without calling them a discovery, then re-ran the analysis with a specific goal: count how many such events existed in two years of data. They found 26 more. That total, not the two, is what the discovery claim rests on.

The process was miserable. The paper took six months or more to write, and in the stretch after the announcement — which was named physics breakthrough of the year — Halzen spent his time worrying he would have to retract.

"Making discoveries is not fun," he says. "And that's always true, actually. It's no fun to be responsible for discoveries."

For anyone managing a high-stakes claim with no independent verification path, that is the playbook: publish the anomaly, do not name it, then design the follow-up analysis that can actually justify the name.

One alert, more than 20 telescopes, and an active galaxy in Orion

After 2013, three years of data showed neutrinos arriving from every direction with no preference. So the team changed the question. Instead of waiting to accumulate a sky map, they built a live alert: the moment IceCube registers a neutrino, an early reconstruction of its direction is sent by Iridium satellite phone to astronomers around the world.

In 2017 a very-high-energy event went out. More than 20 telescopes swung toward the region in Orion. They found an active galaxy — a galaxy whose supermassive black hole is still pulling in matter, spinning up a whirlpool that accelerates infalling particles. The neutrinos trace back to a point directly above the black hole.

Halzen is precise about what that proved. "We have found sources of cosmic rays," he says. "Whether these are the sources of all cosmic rays, we don't know." Other classes of accelerator may still be out there, and finding them may take a bigger detector.

Our own galaxy offers no such engine. Its central black hole has been dormant for at least 10 million years, which Halzen describes as having been decommissioned as a neutrino source.

The durable result is not the Nobel — it is that one experiment became a network

The 2017 identification worked because neutrino data was stitched to electromagnetic observations from instruments that see entirely different things. Halzen places that on a spectrum: radio and gamma rays at one end, gravitational waves at the other, neutrinos alongside them.

"Not only is one experiment impressive, but the combined effect of humans is even better," he says.

He is equally direct about what nobody can forecast. "Making predictions in this business is impossible," he says. "There's no way to predict what will happen." The sky is large, and the instrument has only been looking properly for about a decade.

IceCube 2: ten times the volume, same money after inflation

The proposed next machine expands the instrumented ice around the existing array — which is why the economics are so unusual. IceCube 2 will need about 10,000 sensors, not the 50,000 a like-for-like scale-up would imply, because the modules are more sensitive and the ice is far better understood than it was in 2010.

MetricIceCubeIceCube 2
Instrumented volume1 cubic kilometer~10 cubic kilometers
Sensors required5,160~10,000
Cost, inflation-adjustedBaselineRoughly the same (factor of 1.7 correction)

Halzen frames the division of labor plainly: IceCube's job was to prove the field exists. IceCube 2's job is to find more sources and settle whether the active galaxy found in 2017 is representative or a lucky specimen.

And then there is the waiting game. The most anticipated result in the field — a Milky Way supernova — has no schedule, no budget line, and no way to accelerate. The detector is simply on, and has been since 1994.

Halzen closes on motivation rather than technology. He wants the project to inspire people to keep dreaming, and he wants students to study science for reasons other than salary. That sentiment is easy to skim past, but it is the same logic that produced the machine: the shallow detector that failed at 1 kilometer became the only instrument on Earth that can watch a star collapse from the inside — a reminder for anyone underwriting long-horizon, capital-heavy science that the payoff often arrives from a capability nobody put in the original plan, and that the discipline of not overclaiming is what keeps the institution credible enough to be funded for the next thirty years.
